Vaudeville. An American form of live entertainment from roughly the 1880s through the 1930s featuring a rapid succession of variety acts—singers, dancers, comedians, acrobats, magicians, trained animals—in dedicated theaters. It was the dominant form of theatrical entertainment in the United States before cinema and supplied early film with most of its comedians and physical performers, including Buster Keaton.

Vaudeville circuits, booking networks like the Keith-Albee circuit and Pantages, made entertainment accessible nationwide and developed standardized fifteen to twenty minute acts designed to keep audiences engaged through rapid-fire variety. Buster Keaton's family—his parents Joe and Myra and his siblings—were vaudeville performers. Keaton appeared on stage from early childhood, and the name Buster Keaton came from a famous pratfall he took as a toddler. His parents' act shaped his approach to physical comedy.

Vaudeville acts typically included comedy sketches with strong physical elements. Slapstick, pratfalls, and absurdist situations predominated because they worked across language and class barriers. The transition from vaudeville to cinema during the 1910s through 1930s saw vaudeville's greatest stars—Chaplin, Keaton, and Laurel and Hardy—transfer to film, while cinema's rising popularity gradually starved vaudeville of audiences and financing. Vaudeville's high turnover rate, with new bills weekly, trained performers in rapid-fire gag density, precision timing, and the ability to read and respond to live audience energy—skills that translated directly to silent film's visual precision.

Unlike British music hall, which thrived in working-class venues, American vaudeville served a broader demographic and emphasized family entertainment, which shaped its humor style toward slapstick over bawdiness. The decline of vaudeville was swiftly complete. By 1935 to 1940, the form was essentially extinct, with only a handful of circuits surviving into the 1950s.
